## **<mark>Overview</mark>** 

At the start of 2011, we were bullish in our outlook for precious metals prices. However, we noted that slowing developed world economic activity and European debt concerns could prove problematic. The sell-off at the end of the year was therefore not entirely unexpected but it was deeper than we had previously thought likely, with prices weakening more than expected, and only the gold price recording an annual gain. 

Many of the global concerns which dominated the news in 2011 will be important this year once again and gold might be expected to benefit most amongst the precious metals from the combination of sluggish growth and significant risk. Interest rates in the developed world are extremely unlikely to rise and economic growth is set to be weak (although the USA looks somewhat healthier than had been expected a few months ago). Quantitative easing in the USA looks less likely than before now that the economy there is showing some signs of better health. European debt concerns will be a major influence on the markets whatever happens, with the Euro likely to weaken, although we expect the Euro to continue as a viable currency. Some form of European quantitative easing seems increasingly likely, suggesting that there could be further boosts to a range of asset prices. 

Looking forward into 2012, the new hot topics are US-Iranian tension, the speed of the Chinese economy (and to a lesser extent those of Brazil and India) and the health of the Euro and of the Eurozone. In general, we feel relatively positive about the global economy, expecting a low level of growth despite the challenges faced by the emerging economies, and we expect the Euro to survive. However, there are more negative risks in the macroeconomic environment than potential pleasant surprises. For instance, the worsening of US-Iranian relations could lead to higher oil prices: a short term positive for commodity prices perhaps but a longer term drag on growth. We are, nonetheless, positive once again in our outlook for precious metals prices, albeit from lower levels for palladium, platinum and silver. The prospect of reasonable global economic growth suggests that some capital appreciation might be expected too, particularly where the relevant company is exposed to higher developing world growth. However, risk aversion and high price volatility are likely to make equity investment only for the brave in early 2012 unless equity prices make a determined move higher or price volatility decreases. If this happens, the prospect of equity outperformance could attract some capital from the commodities themselves into the shares of the mining companies. 

Within the commodity sector, last year’s surprisingly weak performance may deter some investors from further speculative activity. However, the negatives associated with other asset markets mean that we still expect to see plenty of active investors in the commodity sector. Here, the investment argument is between cyclical and non-cyclical commodities. Although the global economy is likely to grow – in the absence of a Euro break-up – the pace of growth is set to slow. Less cyclical commodities are likely to be favoured, with gold a potential beneficiary. The other precious metals are more exposed to industrial demand and could underperform gold in this scenario, trading more in line with agricultural commodities or some base metals.

### **The Euro crisis** 

The early December “fiscal compact” or mini-treaty agreed by almost all the member states of the European Union seems to be an attempt to address two separate issues. Firstly, politicians have belatedly realised that a currency union requires some fiscal responsibility. And, where this responsibility is not forthcoming voluntarily, it will have to be mandated. Secondly, the compact appears to be an attempt to reassure Germany in particular that the debtor nations will show a greater level of responsibility. The theory is that this partial loss of sovereignty of the debtor nations is the price to pay for German permission for the ECB to relax its lending rules in order to act as lender of last resort or to accede to proposals of issuing joint Eurobonds. 

The first aim, that of encouraging or mandating fiscal responsibility amongst the member states is an important longer term component of stabilising the Euro and some progress appears to have been made towards this. Unfortunately, the second aim appears not to have been achieved with the rhetoric coming from the German Government and the ECB not having softened at all. As a result, the summit appears to have focused on the longer term problems without addressing the shorter term ones. This is rather like standing on a railway track with a train approaching and writing to your parliamentary representative to argue for better safety on the railways

rather than jumping out of the way of the oncoming train: a reasonable action but not the one required at that time. 

Given that even the fiscal compact is not fully defined and that a number of countries will separately have to ratify any agreement, it still seems likely to us that not every one of the 26 countries which initially signaled their assent will sign a final deal. Depending on the number of those that do finally sign (and whether that includes all of the Eurozone countries) this summit may have achieved little other than alienating the UK. 

However, there are more useful actions taking place within Europe. The ECB has repeatedly insisted that it would not buy sovereign bonds in significant volumes and would not embark upon quantitative easing. However, just before Christmas, it revealed that it had leant over €400 billion in three year funding to Eurozone banks. This should at least ease some of the liquidity problems that have been concerning the market. And, whether or not it qualifies under the technical definition of quantitative easing, it does look very similar to quantitative easing. It is not clear how much of this money will be lent into the real economy or used to buy further sovereign bonds. However, by solving the current liquidity question, it has improved the economic outlook. If this is close enough to “printing money”, then this could be positive for asset prices. However, the size of the funding required should at least cause some concern amongst investors that all is not well with the European economy. 

In any case, the first quarter of 2012 will be an interesting time for the Eurozone. The ratings agencies placed a large number of European countries on negative watch in December and the recent downgrades will add to the economic stress. Additionally, Italy in particular, will hold very large bond auctions in January and February. It is hard to forecast currency movements in this environment but there is certainly substantial downside risk to the Euro against the Dollar in the early part of the year. 

### **Effects of a real Euro crisis** 

Our base case scenario for 2012 assumes that no countries are forced from the Euro and that it survives as a viable currency. If this is the case, it will gradually regain some poise and slow its seven month fall against the US Dollar (although an exchange rate of as low as $1.20 seems entirely possible). 

However, it is important to consider the possibility that a country will fall – or be pushed – from the Euro. Superficially, the most likely candidate to leave the Euro is Greece. Austerity seems not to be working well, with “growth” turning strongly negative. Without

further bailouts and major fiscal changes, which may prove societally unacceptable, Greece will not be able to service its debts and it may therefore be forced to leave the Euro. This would be enormously disrupti

ve to the European economy but should, of itself, be manageable due to the relatively small size of the Greek economy. However, this would place extra pressure on other countries within the Eurozone which are running budget deficits and have large borrowings. Bond yields would rise for Ireland, Italy, Spain and probably even France as the permanence of the Euro came into question. 

It is also possible that other countries could leave the Euro with the negotiation and ratification process for the proposed fiscal compact liable to cause considerable friction between countries. However, the fact that 26 out of 27 EU countries agreed to this outline deal in early December demonstrates the desire to hold the Euro together. This partial resignation of national sovereignty was unimaginable only a few months earlier. Given that this has occurred, and was essentially agreed in only a single day, it seems that politicians may finally be willing to act in the Euro’s interests and we therefore expect the Euro to survive 2012. 

However, should any country leave the Euro, we expect this to lead to a reduction of at least one percentage point in European economic output. Much larger disruptions are possible too in various more depressing scenarios. More importantly, liquidity problems would require the sale of all sorts of assets. We believe that this would be negative for almost all asset prices and poses a low probability but potentially large downside risk to our forecasts. The long term effect of such a move might be positive for Europe’s economy but there would be huge short term problems. 

### **Political constraints on economic action** 

Next year will see a few important elections or other political upheavals. Unfortunately, with these approaching, politicians’ focus tends to move from mundane matters such as ensuring the survival of a currency or presenting widespread economic recession towards the more important question of retaining or gaining power. 

In the Euro zone, the room for political manoeuvre is limited by the forthcoming French presidential elections (which start in April 2012). With this approaching, there seems little prospect of concerted French attempts to move towards a balanced budget in the first few months of the year, since this would involve making unpopular decisions on cutting benefits. The prospect of German federal elections in 2013 makes a fully-fledged, German-funded bail-out of any debtor countries or the issuing of Eurobonds on that timescale very unlikely. Both of these situations suggest that the Eurozone crisis will continue to develop for some time. 

Just as importantly for the global economy, the US Presidential elections will take place in November 2012. Interestingly, sentiment on both sides of the political divide seems to agree that the US needs to make a start on reducing its budget deficit. So, after the elections, whoever wins, we could see a move towards shoring up of the USA’s finances. Unfortunately, b

efore that point, the antagonistic and dysfunctional current nature of American party politics makes it unlikely that significant legislation will be passed. Although the US economy is growing acceptably well at the moment, there are fiscal headwinds approaching next year from the potential expiry of payroll tax cuts and unemployment insurance benefits. These have been temporarily extended and both parties may yet be able to find agreement on extending these measures further. However, if they do not, US economic growth could sink to a lethargic 1-2 per cent this year. 

The third major political issue is the election of the new Chinese Politburo which will take place in Autumn 2012. The Communist Party’s main pre-occupation leading up to this will be to ensure social stability. This will require the taming of inflation and the generation of economic growth. Current figures suggest that inflation is now falling and that the Bank of China may either reduce interest rates or further reduce bank reserve ratio requirements

Looking at the platinum group metals specifically, all of the major producing nations face leadership elections during the coming year. The National Conference of South Africa’s ANC will elect a leader in December 2012. It is not yet clear who the likely winner (and presumably the next leader of South Africa itself) will be. However, given the populist discussion over mine nationalisation, there could be upwards pressure on platinum prices ahead of this vote, regardless of the eventual winner and any policies they may adopt. 

Likewise, Zimbabwe faces an election at some point in 2012. Although current Government policy towards the mining industry seems rather confused, it seems clear that Zanu PF at least favours higher levels of local tax and local ownership of mining operations within Zimbabwe. With an election approaching, this populist, nationalist rhetoric is likely to intensify. This could add to mining costs in Zimbabwe, delay capital expenditure and lead to higher metal prices in the medium term. By contrast, the outcome of the upcoming Russian presidential election seems less likely to have any noticeable impact on platinum group metal production within Russia. 

### **Price seasonality** 

Over the last decade, there has been a reasonable degree of price seasonality for the major precious metals. Typically, prices have performed best during the first and last quarters of a year, on average. The extremely weak price performance of the four main precious metals in Q4 2011 should therefore worry investors in case it is a signal of bearish sentiment developing within this sector. 

In fact, for most of the precious metals (especially gold, palladium

and platinum), we feel that sentiment remains positive for a range of reasons, with expectations of higher prices (although recent meetings have given us a rather more negative prognosis for the silver price in the short term). However, longer term ambition and expectations for higher prices can be badly affected by short term price performance. We therefore find three issues of greatest concern (in terms of price) for the first quarter of 2012. Firstly, the Euro crisis shows little sign of being solved one way or another in the first few months of 2012 if ever. As a result, concerns over the Euro could allow the Dollar to strengthen, placing downwards pressure on commodity prices. We do not expect this trend to last throughout the year but this could drag on commodity prices in the first and second quarters. Most of these central banks are independent and a move to sell gold to finance the national debt would be unconstitutional or at least unconventional even if it fell within the CBGA3 limits for the weight of metal sold. Finally, the sale of gold might in any case be interpreted negatively by the markets, as the last throw of the dice. For all of these reasons, we do not expect significant selling of gold. 

### **Hedging and production** 

2011 was a quiet year for producer hedging in the gold market. Following the burst of dehedging seen leading up to 2010, most of the large miners are now unhedged. A number of smaller hedges have been signed but these are almost universally for project finance. Although we can see a rationale for carrying out some hedging at current prices, the industry remains firmly against hedging for the moment and we do not expect significant hedging activity to emerge in the next year or two. Eventually, we expect that it will become more acceptable or even fashionable but, for the moment, it is no longer a significant influence on the market. 

At the same time, after eleven years of price growth, we are starting to see a supply side response with some new operations coming online to replace ageing first generation mines. For example, in a recent announcement, Goldcorp revealed 2011 production of 2.5 million ounces with forecast 2012 production of 2.6 million ounces. Its targeted output for 2016 is much higher at 4.2 million ounces. At Barrick, work on the Pueblo Viejo and Pascua-Lama mines continues with first production scheduled for this year and next year

This move to grow output is echoed by activities at many other mining companies and should lead to an expansion of supply this year and for the next few years if prices remain at their current high levels. We do not expect this to weigh on gold this year but if prices continue to rise, we will see a gradual slowdown in physical demand, increased mine output and scrap recycling and slower price appreciation. 

### **Gold in India and China and price sensitivity** 

In China and India, two of the key physical markets for gold, this metal plays a dual role as investment and as adornment. Given the strong gold price in local currency terms, a certain amount of price sensitivity is present amongst consumers as financial constraints force them to buy smaller, lighter pieces of jewellery. Investor behaviour tends to be somewhat different with higher prices attracting more investment (although Chinese and Indian investors oft

en behave quite differently to short term price signals). **_Figure 8_** _: Large amounts of gold jewellery are on sale in Dubai for export to the huge Indian market._ A recent visit to Dubai confirmed for us the negative impact of the recent spell of Rupee weakness on gold demand. Despite falling in Dollar terms, gold is at close to record levels in Rupee terms and price sensitivity is depressing consumer demand and encouraging recycling. For the investor, with inflation high and real interest rates negative, there seem to be plenty of reasons to buy gold but a spell of Rupee strength may be required to reinvigorate the physical market. Reports from the Bombay Bullion Association estimate that imports of gold into India were barely 125 tonnes in the final quarter of 2011, only 40 per cent of the figure in Q4 2010. For the year as a whole, hopes that India might purchase 1,000 tonnes of the yellow metal were frustrated as sales dipped, with the final figure being closer to 880 tonnes. This extreme price sensitivity was driven by Rupee weakness despite a falling Dollar gold price. Which metal is next?_ Looking at the ruthenium market, prices dropped substantially during 2011. There is little speculative or investor activity in ruthenium so price movements should normally reflect changes in the supply-demand balance. Having been stable at close to $180 for the first half of the year, the price started to decline in Q3, falling below $100 at the end of the year. Ruthenium demand fell last year as purchasing by the hard disk industry slowed. This did not represent lower usage of the metal but rather a decline in working stocks. We expect demand to improve next year, on the assumption that there will be no further stock reductions, with climbing hard disk output largely responsible. We believe, though, that the ruthenium market is currently in surplus with excess metal available and expect further downward pressure to be applied on the price throughout the first half of 2012 at least. The iridium market is rather less transparent than even the ruthenium market. We have seen indications of good demand for iridium crucibles for crys

tal growing and for iridium for other industrial applications. However, it is not clear that this market is in a fundamental deficit that justifies higher prices. These higher prices may instead have been driven by similar bottlenecks and stockbuilding factors to those that drove ruthenium prices higher in 2006 and 2007. While we do not think it is intellectually reasonable to forecast prices in illiquid markets such as iridium, we are concerned about the longer term sustainability of current iridium prices on a demand basis.
